newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASEAN-EU need wider, more mature relations - panel.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN-EU need wider, more mature relations - panel.

text.p: ASEAN and the European Union (EU) need to develop a more mature relationship and widen their dialogue in politics, security, economics and culture to prepare for the new century, a panel of experts said.

A report by the ASEAN-EU Eminent Persons Group, obtained by Reuters on Thursday, said the past decade of rapid economic and political growth within ASEAN had changed the nature of its relationship with the EU from donor-recipient to one of equals.
ASEAN -- the Association of Southeast Asian Nations -- groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
The group of 16 experts from public and private sectors was formed in 1994 by the ASEAN-EU foreign ministers to draft recommendations for a new ASEAN-EU partnership.
The report is to be discussed at the 12th ASEAN-EU Ministers Meeting in Singapore on February 13-14.

"There is much room for improvement in ASEAN-EU relations because in the past, the emphasis is more on development cooperation...and a narrower economic relationship," Yeo Lay Hwee of the government-linked Institute of Policy Studies in Singapore told Reuters.

"But now, as ASEAN becomes more of a middle-income economy, the relationship should include more dialogue on political and security issues, while the economic relationship must be more mutually beneficial rather than one-sided."

The report expressed concern that economic exchanges between East Asia and Europe had not kept pace with its potential. It showed signs of falling behind trade between East Asia and North America, the report said.
Total ASEAN-EU trade in 1995 was US$99.5 billion, while ASEAN-U.S. trade was nearly $110 billion, according to Singapore Foreign Ministry data.
Concluding that ASEAN-EU trade and investment could be a central dynamo for growth, the report recommended a comprehensive economic approach to boost commercial exchanges.

The plan focused on strong growth and job creation, willingness to lower trade and investment barriers, a common adherence to World Trade Organisation principles and the need for economic ministers to meet more regularly.
It said since the two regional blocs comprise developing and developed countries, they "should help to broker consensus and agreement" between the two groups of economies within the WTO.
The report also called for a stronger relationship on political and security matters involving greater dialogue among the government, private think tanks and academic institutions.
This would involve greater cooperation in United Nations peacekeeping missions and a common front to ensure that member countries meet their financial commitments to the UN.
